act: Right to Information Act 2005
title: RTI — Filing an Information Request
keywords: RTI right to information government file application PIO public information officer fees rejection appeal transparency
plain_text: Any citizen can file an RTI application to any Central or State government department, public authority, or government-funded body. Fee: Rs.10 (waived for BPL families). Submit to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the concerned department. Response time: 30 days (48 hours if it concerns life or liberty). If rejected or no response: File First Appeal to Appellate Authority within 30 days. Second Appeal to Central/State Information Commission within 90 days. Penalty for delay: Rs.250 per day up to Rs.25,000 on PIO personally.

act: Consumer Protection Act 2019
title: Consumer Forum — Filing a Consumer Complaint
keywords: consumer complaint defective product bad service fraud overcharge district forum state commission national commission refund replacement
plain_text: Any consumer can file a complaint against a seller, manufacturer, or service provider for defective goods, deficient service, unfair trade practice, or overcharging. Jurisdiction by claim value: District Commission (up to Rs.1 crore), State Commission (Rs.1–10 crore), National Commission (above Rs.10 crore). No court fee. You can file yourself without a lawyer. Time limit: 2 years from the cause of action. Remedies include refund, replacement, compensation, and punitive damages. E-filing available at: edaakhil.nic.in.

act: Consumer Protection Act 2019
title: CCPA — Unfair Trade Practice and Misleading Ads
keywords: misleading advertisement false claims fake reviews unfair trade practice CCPA product recall
plain_text: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) can investigate unfair trade practices, misleading advertisements, and issue orders for recall of unsafe goods. Complaint can be filed at consumerhelpline.gov.in (National Consumer Helpline: 1915). CCPA can impose penalties up to Rs.10 lakh on manufacturers for misleading ads, and Rs.50 lakh for repeat violations.

act: Industrial Disputes Act 1947 / Code on Industrial Relations 2020
title: Wrongful Termination / Illegal Retrenchment
keywords: wrongful termination fired illegal retrenchment layoff notice period severance pay compensation workman employee dismissed without cause
plain_text: A workman (employee earning under Rs.18,000/month in some states, Rs.25,000 in Code 2020) cannot be retrenched without: 1 month written notice or pay in lieu, retrenchment compensation of 15 days' average pay per year of service, government permission (for establishments with 100+ workers). Illegal retrenchment is an industrial dispute. File complaint with the Labour Commissioner or raise an industrial dispute. Time limit: 3 years.

act: Payment of Wages Act 1936 / Minimum Wages Act 1948
title: Wage Theft — Unpaid or Delayed Wages
keywords: salary not paid unpaid wages wage theft delayed salary employer not paying ESI PF deduction bonus minimum wage
plain_text: Every employer must pay wages on time (before 7th or 10th of following month). Unauthorized deductions are illegal. File complaint with the Payment of Wages Inspector or Labour Commissioner. Also report to the EPFO if PF is not deposited. Minimum Wages Act sets state-wise minimum daily wages — violation is a criminal offence. Claim: full wages + 10x compensation as penalty in some states. EPFO helpline: 1800-118-005.

act: Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1952
title: PF Not Deposited / EPF Withdrawal
keywords: PF provident fund EPF not deposited employer deducting PF but not depositing EPF withdrawal UAN passbook
plain_text: If your employer is deducting PF from your salary but not depositing it with EPFO, this is a criminal offence. File complaint at the EPFO regional office or online at epfindia.gov.in. Also file with the Labour Commissioner. Employer can face prosecution under Section 14 (imprisonment up to 3 years + fine). For withdrawing your PF: log in to UAN portal (unifiedportal-mem.epfindia.gov.in) and submit Form 19/10C. EPFO helpline: 1800-118-005.

act: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013 (POSH Act)
title: Sexual Harassment at Workplace — POSH Complaint
keywords: POSH sexual harassment workplace office boss colleague unwanted touch comment inappropriate manager HR complaint ICC
plain_text: Any woman (including contract, temporary, or domestic workers) can file a complaint for sexual harassment at the workplace. Complaint must be filed within 3 months of the incident. Every organisation with 10+ employees must have an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC). If no ICC exists or the harasser is the employer, file with the Local Complaints Committee (LCC) at the District level. The committee must complete inquiry within 60 days. Penalty on employer for not having ICC: Rs.50,000. The employer is bound by the committee's recommendations. The victim's identity is protected.

act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
title: Domestic Violence — Protection Order and Rights
keywords: domestic violence husband abuse wife partner assault threat home beaten DV act protection order shelter maintenance
plain_text: Domestic violence includes physical, sexual, verbal, emotional, and economic abuse. The victim (wife, live-in partner, sister, mother) can apply to a Magistrate for: Protection Order (preventing abuser from contacting or harassing), Residence Order (right to stay in shared home), Monetary Relief (maintenance, medical expenses, losses), Custody Order. File complaint with Protection Officer (at Collectorate/SDM office) or directly in Magistrate's Court. Interim orders can be passed within 3 days of application. Violation of Protection Order is a criminal offence (imprisonment up to 1 year or fine). National Women's Helpline: 181. Domestic Violence Helpline: 1091.

act: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 / BNS Section 84 / IPC Section 498A
section: BNS Section 84 / IPC Section 498A / Dowry Prohibition Act Section 3, 4
title: Dowry Harassment and Cruelty by Husband/In-laws
keywords: dowry harassment cruelty husband in-laws IPC 498A matrimonial cruelty wife abuse demand gold jewellery property harassment for dowry
plain_text: Cruelty by husband or his relatives (demand for dowry, harassment, threats) is a cognizable, non-bailable offence. Punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. Giving or taking dowry is also an offence under the Dowry Prohibition Act (up to 5 years imprisonment). The woman can also claim protection under the Domestic Violence Act simultaneously. File FIR at nearest police station. A female officer must record the statement. Complaint can also be filed directly before a Magistrate. National Women's Helpline: 181.

act: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012 (POCSO)
title: Child Sexual Abuse — POCSO Complaint
keywords: POCSO child abuse sexual child minor under 18 molest assault reporting teacher relative neighbour
plain_text: POCSO protects all children (below 18) from sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography. Any person aware of such an offence is LEGALLY REQUIRED to report it to the police or SJPU (Special Juvenile Police Unit). Failure to report is a punishable offence. The child's identity must never be disclosed. The case is tried in a Special Court with a child-friendly environment. Accused is presumed guilty unless proven innocent (reverse burden of proof). Bail is not easily granted. Childline helpline: 1098 (24x7, free). File FIR at any police station.

act: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989
title: SC/ST Atrocities — Caste-Based Discrimination and Violence
keywords: caste discrimination atrocity SC ST dalit untouchability slur verbal abuse physical assault caste based violence denial of rights
plain_text: The SC/ST Atrocities Act provides special protection against caste-based crimes including: abusing in public using caste names, physical assault, land grabbing, social boycott, bonded labour, denial of water/food in public places. Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts try these cases. Complaint to police: an FIR MUST be registered immediately (police cannot refuse). Failure to register FIR is itself a punishable offence. Special public prosecutors appointed. Victim is entitled to compensation, rehabilitation, and witnesses are protected. No anticipatory bail for the accused normally. Helpline: 14566 (National SC/ST Commission).

act: Transfer of Property Act 1882 / Rent Control Acts (State-specific)
section: Section 108 TPA / State Rent Control Acts
title: Tenant Rights — Illegal Eviction, Lockout, and Rent Disputes
keywords: tenant rent eviction landlord lock out illegal eviction notice to quit rental agreement security deposit dispute possession
plain_text: A landlord CANNOT evict a tenant without a court order. Changing locks or cutting utilities (water, electricity) to force eviction is illegal and punishable under BNS/IPC (criminal trespass, mischief). Rights: Right to peaceful enjoyment of property, right to basic utilities, right to written receipt for rent, right to recover security deposit. For wrongful eviction: File FIR under BNS Section 329 (criminal trespass). File civil suit for injunction and possession. Approach Rent Control Authority (in most states). Notice period before eviction: varies by state (typically 1–6 months). Always keep rent receipts and rental agreement safely.

act: Registration Act 1908 / Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988
title: Property Registration and Unregistered Documents
keywords: property registration unregistered sale deed gift deed property dispute land dispute encroachment benami stamp duty
plain_text: Any transfer of immovable property worth more than Rs.100 must be registered. Unregistered sale deeds for immovable property are not valid in court. Stamp duty and registration fees must be paid at the correct rate (varies by state — typically 5–7% of market value). Benami property (held in another's name) can be confiscated by the government. For property disputes: File a civil suit for declaration/possession in the civil court. Approach revenue authorities for land record disputes. Time limit for civil property suits: 12 years from dispossession.

act: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 / Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal
title: Motor Accident — Insurance Claim and Compensation
keywords: accident road accident vehicle hit car bike motor accident insurance claim compensation hospital MACT tribunal third party
plain_text: Victims of motor accidents can claim compensation from the at-fault driver's third-party insurance. File claim at the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) in the district. No court fee for accident victims. Claim can be filed even if the vehicle is uninsured or is a hit-and-run (Solatium Fund). Time limit: 6 months to apply; there is no absolute bar after 6 months if sufficient cause is shown. No-fault liability: Rs.50,000 (death), Rs.25,000 (grievous injury) available without proving negligence. Preserve: FIR copy, medical bills, discharge summary, photographs, witness names. Report to police: mandatory within 24 hours.

act: Information Technology Act 2000 / IT (Amendment) Act 2008
title: Cybercrime — Identity Theft, Deepfake, Revenge Porn
keywords: cybercrime identity theft fake account impersonation morphed photo video nude fake account hacked social media revenge porn deepfake online abuse
plain_text: Section 66C: Identity theft (using someone's password, digital signature, biometric) — up to 3 years + Rs.1 lakh fine. Section 66D: Cheating by impersonation online — up to 3 years + Rs.1 lakh fine. Section 66E: Violation of privacy by capturing/publishing private images — up to 3 years + Rs.2 lakh fine. Section 67A/67B: Publishing obscene/sexually explicit content (including of minors) online — up to 5 years. Report at cybercrime.gov.in (National Cybercrime Reporting Portal) or call 1930 (Cybercrime Helpline). For revenge porn / non-consensual intimate images: also invoke BNS Section 357C. Request platform takedown immediately.

act: Information Technology Act 2000
title: Hacking, Data Theft, and Unauthorized Access
keywords: hacking hacked account password stolen data breach unauthorized access phishing email fraud banking fraud OTP fraud
plain_text: Unauthorized access to a computer, system, or network is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to Rs.5 lakh. Data theft (dishonestly receiving stolen computer data) — up to 3 years + fine. For banking fraud via OTP/phishing: Report to bank immediately, freeze account, file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in and call 1930. Under RBI guidelines: if reported within 3 working days, zero liability on customer for unauthorized electronic transactions. Keep all phishing emails, SMS, and call records as evidence.

act: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881
title: Cheque Bounce — Filing a Criminal Complaint
keywords: cheque bounce dishonour returned cheque 138 NI act 30 days notice legal notice criminal case court money recovery
plain_text: If a cheque is dishonoured (bounced) for insufficient funds or account closed: Step 1 — Send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of dishonour. Step 2 — If payment not made within 15 days of receiving notice, file criminal complaint in Magistrate's Court within 30 days of expiry of 15-day period. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years OR fine up to twice the cheque amount OR both. This is a compoundable offence (can be settled). Also file civil suit for recovery separately. Keep: original cheque, bank memo of dishonour, copy of notice with postal proof.

act: Limitation Act 1963
title: Limitation Periods — Deadlines for Filing Cases in India
keywords: limitation period deadline time limit file case court suit civil suit FIR complaint when to file how long
plain_text: KEY LEGAL DEADLINES: Civil suit for property recovery: 12 years. Civil suit for money recovery (contract): 3 years from breach. Consumer complaint: 2 years from cause of action. Motor accident claim: 6 months (no absolute bar with cause shown). Cheque bounce (NI Act 138): File within 30 days after notice period expires. FIR: No limitation for serious offences; some minor offences have time bars. Domestic violence complaint: No limitation. POCSO: No limitation. RTI appeal: 30/90 days. NOTE: Courts can condone (excuse) delay if 'sufficient cause' is shown. Always act quickly — delay weakens your case even when legally permissible.

act: Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973 / Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023
title: FIR — Your Rights When Filing a First Information Report
keywords: FIR first information report police refusing to register complaint zero FIR station house officer how to file FIR rights
plain_text: You have the RIGHT to file an FIR at any police station for a cognizable offence. Police CANNOT refuse to register an FIR for cognizable offences. If refused: file a written complaint to the SP/DSP; file complaint before the Magistrate (Section 156(3) CrPC); file at any other police station (Zero FIR). Zero FIR: Any police station must register an FIR regardless of jurisdiction and transfer it to the correct station. You are entitled to a FREE copy of the FIR. Police must begin investigation immediately for cognizable offences. Bribery for FIR registration: complaint to Anti-Corruption Bureau.

act: Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973 / BNSS 2023
title: Arrest Rights — What Police Can and Cannot Do
keywords: arrest rights police rights illegal detention custody rights police harassment handcuff bail right to lawyer informed of charges
plain_text: RIGHTS ON ARREST: Police must inform you of the grounds of arrest. You have the RIGHT to inform a relative or friend. Police must produce you before a Magistrate within 24 hours. You have the RIGHT to consult and be defended by a lawyer of your choice. Police cannot detain you beyond 24 hours without Magistrate's order. Handcuffing: Allowed only in exceptional circumstances (escape risk, violent accused). Police cannot torture, humiliate, or abuse you in custody. Any torture or custodial death is a human rights violation — file complaint with NHRC or State Human Rights Commission. Women: Cannot be arrested after sunset and before sunrise (except under exceptional circumstances with female officer present).

act: Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) / BNSS 2023
title: Bail — Bailable and Non-Bailable Offences
keywords: bail arrested bail application anticipatory bail non bailable offence police station magistrate court high court session court
plain_text: BAILABLE offences: You have a RIGHT to bail from the police station itself. NON-BAILABLE offences: Bail is at the court's discretion; apply before Magistrate. Anticipatory Bail (Section 438): Applied for BEFORE arrest in anticipation of arrest. Filed in Sessions Court or High Court. If granted, police cannot arrest you for that offence. Surety bail: A person who pledges property/money as guarantee for your appearance. Regular bail: Applied after arrest before the Magistrate, Sessions Court, or High Court. Free legal aid for bail: Contact DLSA at the district court. NALSA helpline: 15100.

act: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987
section: Section 12 — Entitlement to Free Legal Aid
title: Free Legal Aid — Who Qualifies and How to Get It
keywords: free legal aid lawyer free NALSA DLSA SLSA eligible legal aid annual income SC ST woman child victim how to get free lawyer
plain_text: FREE LEGAL AID IS A RIGHT under Article 39A of the Constitution. You qualify if you are: a woman, a child, a person with disability, an SC/ST member, a victim of trafficking, a person in custody, or your annual income is below Rs.3 lakh (Central) or as set by your State. How to get it: Walk into any District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at your district court. Call NALSA helpline: 15100. Apply online at nalsa.gov.in. You will be assigned a panel lawyer free of charge. DLSA also provides: legal advice, Lok Adalat services (out-of-court settlement), and victim compensation.

act: Lok Adalat — Legal Services Authorities Act 1987
title: Lok Adalat — Out of Court Settlement
keywords: lok adalat out of court settlement fast track dispute resolution cheap court alternative motor accident cheque bounce electricity bill
plain_text: Lok Adalats provide a platform for out-of-court settlement. Cases that can be settled: Motor accident claims, cheque bounce (NI Act), labour disputes, matrimonial disputes (except divorce), electricity disputes, land acquisition disputes, and most civil matters. Benefits: No court fees (refunded if already paid), settlement is final and binding like a court decree, no appeal is possible, very fast resolution (usually same day). How to access: Contact NALSA (15100), your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA), or any state legal services authority. The parties must agree to settlement voluntarily.

act: The Workmen's Compensation Act 1923 / Employees' Compensation Act
title: Workplace Injury — Workers' Compensation Claim
keywords: workplace accident injury factory accident construction fall machinery accident workers compensation disability death at work
plain_text: If a worker suffers an injury (or death) arising out of and in the course of employment, the employer is liable to pay compensation regardless of negligence. Compensation for death: 50% of monthly wages x relevant factor (based on age) or Rs.1.20 lakh minimum. Compensation for total disablement: 60% of wages x relevant factor or Rs.1.40 lakh minimum. File claim before the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation (at Labour Court/Commissioner's office). Also file FIR if the accident was caused by employer's gross negligence. Employer must report the accident within 7 days.

act: Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 (FSSAI)
title: Food Safety — Adulterated or Unsafe Food Complaint
keywords: adulterated food food poisoning bad food expired food restaurant hotel hygiene FSSAI complaint unsafe food
plain_text: If you are a victim of food poisoning or find adulterated food: File a complaint at the state Food Safety Commissioner's office or FSSAI. Call FSSAI helpline: 1800-11-4000. Also file a consumer complaint at the District Consumer Commission. For serious food poisoning involving hospitalization: file FIR under BNS/IPC (cheating, negligence) + complaint to FSSAI. Penalty for selling adulterated food: fine up to Rs.10 lakh + imprisonment up to life if food causes death. Keep the food sample sealed if possible as evidence. Take photographs. Get medical records of food poisoning treatment.

act: Environment Protection Act 1986 / National Green Tribunal Act 2010
title: Environmental Violations — Noise, Pollution, Industrial Dumping
keywords: pollution noise complaint factory smoke industrial waste NGT national green tribunal environment complaint air water noise pollution
plain_text: For environmental violations (industrial pollution, noise, illegal construction near water bodies, solid waste dumping): File complaint with the State Pollution Control Board (SPCB). Approach the National Green Tribunal (NGT) at ngt.nic.in — any person can file a petition for environmental harm. Noise pollution: File complaint with local police (under Noise Pollution Rules 2000, permissible limits are 55 dB day / 45 dB night in residential areas). Polluter must pay compensation for environmental damage caused. NGT can award compensation and direct remediation. Filing at NGT: No court fee for original applications, nominal fee for appeals.

act: Electricity Act 2003
title: Electricity Dispute — Wrong Bill, Illegal Disconnection, Theft Allegation
keywords: electricity bill wrong high electricity bill illegal disconnection power cut meter tampering allegation electricity theft complaint DISCOM
plain_text: For wrong or excessively high electricity bill: First send a written complaint to the DISCOM (Distribution Company) Assistant Engineer/Executive Engineer. If unresolved, file complaint with the State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) or Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (CGRF) of the DISCOM — free of charge. Also file a consumer complaint at District Consumer Forum. Electricity cannot be disconnected without 15 days' notice for dues. Illegal disconnection: Demand reconnection in writing; if refused, approach CGRF/Consumer Forum. Meter reading dispute: Request for meter testing (small fee refunded if meter is found faulty). Electricity theft allegation: You can appeal the demand notice before the DISCOM's designated authority.

act: Specific Relief Act 1963
title: Injunction — Stopping Someone from Doing Something Immediately
keywords: injunction stop someone restraining order urgent court order demolition eviction encroachment stop construction stay order
plain_text: An injunction is a court order directing a person to stop or continue doing a specific act. Types: Temporary Injunction (during court proceedings), Permanent Injunction (final), Mandatory Injunction (compelling an act). Applied for in civil court. URGENT situations: You can apply for an ex-parte (without notice to other side) temporary injunction if immediate harm is shown. Common uses: Stop illegal eviction, stop demolition of property, stop encroachment, preserve status quo during property disputes. Court considers: Prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable harm. Can be granted the same day in emergencies.

act: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 (IBC)
title: Personal Insolvency — Excessive Debt and Loan Default
keywords: debt loan default unable to repay personal insolvency bankruptcy lender harassment recovery agent threatening loan NPA
plain_text: If you are unable to repay loans: Creditors (banks, NBFCs) must follow RBI guidelines on recovery — no threatening calls, no harassment, no visits at odd hours. For harassment: File complaint with RBI (rbi.org.in/Scripts/Complaints.aspx) and Banking Ombudsman (free). If debt exceeds Rs.1,000 and you cannot pay: apply for Personal Insolvency Resolution Process at the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) or Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). One-time settlement (OTS): Banks often offer this — negotiate directly. Credit Information report dispute: File with CIBIL/Experian for incorrect entries.

act: Senior Citizens Act (Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007)
title: Senior Citizens — Maintenance and Property Rights
keywords: senior citizen elderly parent maintenance abandonment property transfer eviction adult child neglect old age home
plain_text: Children and heirs are legally obligated to maintain parents and senior citizens (Section 4). Maintenance up to Rs.10,000/month can be ordered by the Maintenance Tribunal (Sub-Divisional Magistrate). Property transferred by a senior citizen can be CANCELLED if the recipient fails to provide basic amenities and physical needs (Section 23). Senior citizens can apply to reclaim such property before the Tribunal. Police/District Administration duty: Protect senior citizens from abuse and neglect. Senior Citizen Helpline: 14567 (Elderline, free, national). Senior citizens cannot be evicted from their own home by children.

act: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act 1985 (NDPS Act)
title: NDPS — Drug Possession and Wrongful Search Rights
keywords: NDPS drugs arrested drug case marijuana ganja heroin possession search seizure wrongful arrest planted drugs rights during search
plain_text: NDPS cases carry very severe punishments (minimum 10 years for commercial quantity). Your RIGHTS during an NDPS search: Police MUST give you the option to be searched before a Magistrate or Gazetted Officer (Section 50 — failure to comply VITIATES the prosecution's case). Any search of a dwelling requires a Magistrate's search warrant. Bail: Generally not available for commercial quantity cases. Small quantity (personal consumption): Rigorous imprisonment up to 1 year or fine. Key defence: Police failure to follow mandatory procedures (Section 50, 57). Always demand proper procedure, write everything down, tell a family member immediately.

act: Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 / Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013
title: Corruption — Reporting Bribery by Government Officials
keywords: bribery corruption government official public servant demand bribe CBI Lokpal Lokayukta anti-corruption ACB trap case
plain_text: Demanding or accepting a bribe is a criminal offence for any public servant under the Prevention of Corruption Act. Punishment: 3 to 7 years imprisonment + fine. How to report: File complaint with the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) of your state. For Central government officials: CBI or Lokpal (lokpal.nic.in). For state officials: State Lokayukta. You can request a TRAP: ACB will set up a trap to catch the official accepting the bribe. NEVER pay a bribe if you can avoid it. If you have already paid: File complaint immediately — delay weakens your case. Whistleblower protection: Whistleblowers Protection Act 2014 protects identity and provides legal safeguards.

act: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act 2016
title: Aadhaar — Data Privacy and Misuse of Biometrics
keywords: aadhaar misuse biometric theft identity fraud aadhaar linked account aadhaar enabled payment system fingerprint misuse
plain_text: No one can compel you to give your Aadhaar for non-notified purposes (only government subsidies and mandated services). Sharing your Aadhaar number without consent is an offence. Biometric data cannot be used for any purpose other than authentication. If your Aadhaar is misused (bank account linked without consent, AePS fraud): Lock your biometrics at myaadhaar.uidai.gov.in or UIDAI app. File complaint with UIDAI at help@uidai.gov.in or 1947 (toll-free). Also file cybercrime complaint at 1930 and with your bank. Your Virtual ID (VID) can be used instead of Aadhaar number to protect privacy.

act: Mental Healthcare Act 2017
title: Mental Health — Rights of Persons with Mental Illness
keywords: mental illness rights treatment psychiatry hospital admission forced detention mental health law rights
plain_text: Every person with mental illness has the right to access mental healthcare, to be treated with dignity, to confidentiality, to legal aid, and to make advance directives for treatment. Involuntary admission to a mental health facility requires approval of the Mental Health Review Board. Restraint or seclusion is permitted only in emergencies. Abuse of persons in mental health establishments is a criminal offence. Suicide is decriminalised — a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under mental stress, not criminal. Free mental healthcare: available at government hospitals. NIMHANS Helpline: 080-46110007. Vandrevala Foundation: 1860-2662-345 (24x7).

act: Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act 1995 / RPWD Act 2016
title: Disability Rights — Employment, Reservation and Accessibility
keywords: disability rights disabled person wheelchair ramp reservation employment discrimination workplace accommodation RPWD differently abled
plain_text: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 recognises 21 disabilities. Key rights: 5% reservation in government jobs, 5% in higher education, accessible infrastructure (ramps, lifts, braille), right to vote, right to legal capacity. Discrimination in employment on grounds of disability is a criminal offence (fine up to Rs.10,000; Rs.50,000 for repeat). Private establishments with 20+ employees must employ persons with benchmark disabilities. Harassment or denial of rights: File complaint with the State Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities. Free legal aid is available. Disability Commissioner's offices are in every state capital.

act: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015
title: Juvenile Justice — Rights of Children in Conflict with Law
keywords: juvenile minor arrested child in conflict with law JJB juvenile justice board bail observation home POCSO accused child
plain_text: A child (below 18 years) cannot be tried in an adult criminal court except for heinous offences (minimum 7 years punishment) where the Juvenile Justice Board may transfer 16–18-year-olds after assessment. For all other offences: child appears before the Juvenile Justice Board, not a magistrate. Child cannot be sent to jail. Child in conflict with law is entitled to bail, legal aid, and must be kept in an Observation Home, not a lockup. Identity of the child cannot be disclosed. Childline helpline: 1098. The focus of JJ Act is REFORM, not punishment.

act: Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 (FEMA)
title: FEMA — Foreign Money Transfers and Exchange Violations
keywords: FEMA foreign exchange remittance money from abroad NRI hawala illegal foreign currency FEMA violation foreign investment
plain_text: FEMA regulates foreign exchange transactions for residents of India. Key rules: Individuals can remit up to USD 250,000 per year abroad under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS). Receiving foreign money: permitted under RBI guidelines for personal remittances, investments, and gifts. Hawala (illegal money transfer): criminal offence. NRIs/PIOs: can maintain NRE, NRO, FCNR accounts. FEMA violations: civil penalties (up to 3x the amount involved). Criminal action only for willful violations. Complaints about FEMA violations: Enforcement Directorate (ED). Note: FEMA is civil in nature; ED uses PMLA (money laundering) for criminal prosecution.

act: Maharashtra Rent Control Act 1999 / Delhi Rent Control Act 1958 (State-specific examples)
title: State Rent Control — Tenant Protections (State-Specific)
keywords: rent control act Maharashtra Delhi UP Karnataka Tamil Nadu tenant protection rent increase eviction law state specific
plain_text: Most Indian states have their own Rent Control Acts that limit rent increases and regulate eviction. COMMON PROVISIONS: Landlord cannot increase rent more than prescribed limit (typically 4–10% per year depending on state). Eviction only on specific grounds: non-payment of rent, sub-letting without permission, nuisance, bona fide need of landlord, property in dilapidated condition. All evictions require a court/tribunal order. States with strong tenant protection: Maharashtra, Delhi, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal. States that have moved to model tenancy acts: These allow rent increase by agreement but still require court orders for eviction. IMPORTANT: Register your rental agreement to protect yourself. Approach Rent Controller (at city civil court or sub-registrar office).
